Here is one run of an agent optimizer, in two numbers. By its own logs it
is a textbook success: across the run its best candidate's score on the
development split climbs from 0.582 to 0.685 — +10.3 points, earned
step by step, each new selection beating the last. Scored on a sealed
test split the method never saw, the same candidates walk from 0.545 down
to 0.461 — −8.5 points. **The optimizer made its agent worse, watched its
own metric rise the whole time, and certified its worst candidate as its
best.**

Nothing about this run is broken, and that is the point. The agent's
per-task behavior is stochastic; the dev signal averages too few samples
of it; and **selecting the maximum of noisy estimates *manufactures*
improvement — no real progress required** — a mechanism decision analysis
named the **optimizer's curse** [@smith-winkler-2006] two decades before
the first prompt optimizer existed. In this post we take that one run
apart, item by item, and show the curse accounts for most of its claimed
lift. The consequence generalizes well beyond this run:
**dev-reported gains from agent optimizers are inflated by default, and a
selection rule that ignores its own noise cannot even keep a run from
going backwards.** This is a companion piece to [our main
evaluation](../the-benchmark/index.qmd), where the same gap shows up
across the whole grid.

## The score climbs no matter what the agent does

The run is Meta-Harness on τ²-bench (airline domain), from our frontier
grid: a meta-agent edits the worker agent's instructions and tools, a dev
evaluation scores each candidate on 55 tasks × 3 reps, and the best dev
score to date decides which candidate survives. @fig-case-curve replays
the run's eleven dev evaluations. The circled ones are its five selection
decisions — the evaluations where the reigning best was dethroned.

![The case run's dev evaluations in order. Circles mark the selection
steps — evaluations where the running best was dethroned. The sealed test
scores the same five selected candidates. (Candidate identity here is
content-verified against the executed agent trees, not the run's own stamp
labels, which carry an off-by-one.)](figures/case_curve.png){#fig-case-curve width=88%}

And here is the evidence each circled decision rested on. Each wide row is
one selected candidate's dev evaluation — one cell per task, shaded by how
many of its three reps passed. The thin row under it is what changed at
that selection step: green improved, red regressed.

{{< include _run_anatomy.qmd >}}

Two things about this run, and both are visible above:

- **The dev score inflates no matter what is measured.** Every one of the
  ten dev evaluations after the seed's — whichever candidate was on the
  bench, kept or rejected — landed above the seed's 0.582. Meanwhile the
  sealed test of the selected chain walks from 0.545 to 0.461. A signal that
  flatters every candidate is not measuring the candidates.
- **The three reps barely agree on what changed.** Each selection step
  rests on ~30 of 55 tasks changing — in both directions at once (+17/−12,
  +15/−13, +16/−16, +16/−12) — for a net of +2 to +8 reps out of 165. At
  the final, decisive step (c008 → c045), not one of the 28 changes is
  unanimous: no task went 0/3 → 3/3 or the reverse. Nothing was solved;
  the dice moved.

The climb is noise; the decline is not. A fresh 3-rep test evaluation of
an unchanged agent moves by 2.4–3.4 points at one standard deviation, so
a drop of 8.5 has probability at most 0.02. **The selection did not
merely fail to find improvement — it certified a genuine regression as
its best.**

## Every measurement disagrees with itself

That zero is not one run's bad luck; it is what the evidence under a
selection decision typically looks like. Across all 41 runs in our grid
— 2,447 pairs of successive dev evaluations — take every task the
previous evaluation scored unanimously, 3/3 or 0/3. When such a task
changes at the next evaluation, the reps almost never agree
(@fig-rep-venn): 6.5% of degradations and 10.5% of improvements are
unanimous — about four and three per comparison, so **the median
selection decision is made without a single change all three reps agree
on.**

![Every task the previous dev evaluation scored unanimously — 3/3 correct
(left) or 0/3 (right) — and that changed at the next evaluation, across all
41 runs. The circles are the next evaluation's three reps; area is the share
of instances. A change the whole evaluation agrees on would sit in the
center — 6.5% of degradations and 10.5% of improvements do. In the median
candidate comparison, not a single change is
unanimous.](figures/rep_venn.png){#fig-rep-venn width=100%}

How much of this churn would an *unchanged* agent produce? Give each task
a fixed pass probability and simply re-roll its three reps: that alone
changes ~23–26 tasks per comparison (observed: 28–32) and moves the dev
score with a standard deviation of about 4 points. Against that null,
every dev gain the case run acted on was indistinguishable from
re-measuring the same agent:

| step | dev Δ | z vs. unchanged agent |
|---|---|---|
| seed → c001 | +4.8pp | +1.1 |
| c001 → c007 | +1.2pp | +0.3 |
| c007 → c008 | +1.8pp | +0.5 |
| c008 → c045 | +2.4pp | +0.6 |

: The case run's four selection steps against the unchanged-agent null.
Every dev gain the method acted on sits within 1.1σ of pure
re-measurement noise. {#tbl-null}

Nor is the case run an unlucky draw: grid-wide, 89% of the 2,447 dev
score changes fall inside ±2σ of the same-agent null
(@fig-grid-consistency) — a signal that mostly carried no information
about the candidates.

![Every change in dev score between successive candidate
evaluations, all 41 frontier runs (2,447 changes): what the methods
measured (colored) vs. what they would have measured re-scoring the
*same unchanged agent* — each task passes with some probability, and
3 reps × ~60 tasks re-rolls those dice (dashed). The signal the methods
optimized on is nearly indistinguishable from the
dice.](figures/grid_consistency.png){#fig-grid-consistency width=100%}

This is where the curse closes. Replay the run with every candidate
secretly an identical copy of the seed — one dev evaluation each, keep
the best. Max-selection over that pure noise "earns" +5 to +7 points of
dev climb, and reaches the observed +10.3 with probability up to 0.2.
**Half to two-thirds of the climb was guaranteed before the method
changed anything** — the textbook optimizer's curse
[@smith-winkler-2006; @thaler-1988]: pick the maximum of noisy estimates,
and the winner is inflated by construction.

## The tax scales with how often you look

Is the tax the same for every optimizer? No — it is priced by how often
the method looks. Averaged over every traced run in our grid, the
methods differ enormously in how many full dev evaluations they take a
maximum over — AdaEvolve ~5 per run, AFlow ~22, Meta-Harness ~31, GEPA
~94 — and the simulated tax follows, from +2.0 points for the method
that looks least to +4.0 for the one that looks most
(@fig-method-curse). The sealed test honors that accounting: the raw
dev climb *misranks* the methods, while climb minus tax roughly
recovers the sealed order — for GEPA the books balance to the decimal
(+0.5 excess, +0.6 sealed).

To be clear, the tax is a fee for looking, not a verdict on any
method's search — where the fee lands depends on the headroom it is
spent against. On GPQA, where no method in our grid finds real lift,
GEPA's +3.5 climb is all tax and its sealed lift is −1.5; on CharXiv,
where headroom exists, the same method's climb clears its tax and the
seal pays out the difference (+1.7). **The curse doesn't say
eval-hungry methods can't win; it says their dev climbs carry the
largest built-in markup — and only the part above it is real.**
(Worker and bench mixes differ per method and the ns are small — read
the ordering, not the decimals.)

![Four methods, averaged over every traced run in our grid (three
benches, all workers), ordered by how many full dev evaluations each
takes a maximum over. Left bar of each pair: the mean dev climb, split
into the part selection noise alone manufactures for that run's own
evaluation count over an *unchanged* seed (gray) and the excess above it
(blue). Right bar: the mean sealed-test lift. The gray tax grows with how
often the method looks; the sealed lift tracks the excess, not the
climb.](figures/method_curse.png){#fig-method-curse width=88%}

The mechanism is three beats. The optimizer's edits do move true quality
— modestly, both ways. The dev signal, a few dozen tasks at three reps,
is saturated by worker stochasticity and cannot rank those movements.
And max-selection manufactures +5–7 points of paper gain while blocking
no regression — **the run random-walks in quality while its own metric
applauds.** The trap was named decades before the first prompt
optimizer, in oil-lease auctions and decision analysis
[@capen-1971; @smith-winkler-2006]; the remedies are as old: enough reps
to resolve the difference being claimed, acceptance rules that know
their own noise, and reading every dev-reported lift net of the tax.
Our grid's mean claimed lifts — +8.8 points on τ², +4.4 on GPQA — are
about what the curse hands out for free.
